fresh-08.question: What did the most recent IPCC report conclude?
fresh-08.answer:
The latest IPCC assessment – the Sixth Assessment Report (AR 6) synthesis completed in March 2023 – concluded that **human influence on the climate system is now unprecedented and is already causing widespread, rapid and intensifying changes across the whole planet**.  Observed changes are “unprecedented in thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of years,” and many of them (e.g., sea‑level rise) are irreversible on centuries‑to‑millennia timescales[5].  

The report warns that **the window to keep global warming to 1.5 °C is rapidly closing**; without immediate, rapid and large‑scale reductions in greenhouse‑gas emissions, limiting warming to close to 1.5 °C – and even 2 °C – will be beyond reach[5].  It also stresses that the world is “on a razor’s edge” with respect to breaching major tipping points, and that urgent, far‑reaching climate action is required to avoid permanent and, in some cases, irreversible damage[1].  

Finally, the synthesis highlighted the need for **conserving roughly 30 %–50 % of Earth’s land, freshwater and ocean areas** (including near‑natural ecosystems) to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem‑service resilience[4].

The Great Wall of China is an ancient series of walls and fortifications, totaling more than 13,000 miles in length, located in northern China. Perhaps the most recognizable symbol of China and its long and vivid history, the Great Wall was originally conceived by Emperor Qin Shi Huang in the third century B.C. as a means of preventing incursions from barbarian nomads. The best-known and best-preserved section of the Great Wall was built in the 14th through 17th centuries A.D., during the Ming [...] Made mostly of earth and stone, the wall stretched from the China Sea port of Shanhaiguan over 3,000 miles west into Gansu province. In some strategic areas, sections of the wall overlapped for maximum security (including the Badaling stretch, north of Beijing, that was later restored during the Ming Dynasty).

From a base of 15 to 50 feet, the Great Wall rose some 15-30 feet high and was topped by ramparts 12 feet or higher; guard towers were distributed at intervals along it. [...] The Bei Qi kingdom (550–577) built or repaired more than 900 miles of wall, and the short-lived but effective Sui Dynasty (581–618) repaired and extended the Great Wall of China a number of times.

With the fall of the Sui and the rise of the Tang Dynasty, the Great Wall lost its importance as a fortification, as China had defeated the Tujue tribe to the north and expanded past the original frontier protected by the wall.
